source: Singh (2026) When Does Belief-Based Agent Memory Help? (Nous), full text
finding: Gap 2, head to head on signals for which claim to trust. On a synthetic contradiction and staleness benchmark, a Bayesian update with per-claim reliability read from hedging language beat recency (last-write-wins) and frequency. It lost where confidence was inverted.
numbers: 60 scenarios, 5 regimes. Realistic macro accuracy: reliability-weighted 100, last-write-wins 67, most-frequent 46, append-and-let-an-LLM-read-all 90. Adversarial (inverted confidence) regime: reliability-weighted 0, last-write-wins 42, frequency 50, append 17. Belief-layer simulation with constant reliability: Bayesian 67.1 vs last-write-wins 73.5; with varying true reliability: Bayesian 100 vs 74.3 vs 48.2. Extractor: confident phrasing 0.95, hedged 0.23.
quote: helps only when epistemic confidence tracks correctness, the common pragmatic case, and hurts when it is inverted
limits: Single author, synthetic data, confidence-correctness link built in by design in four of five regimes. Not a free-running agent. Executed-output provenance was not one of the signals compared here (see d02).
agent_relevance: Recency alone is a weak entrenchment rule. Stated confidence helps only when it tracks truth and fails when inverted. Use it only as a secondary signal under a provenance rule.

source: Singh (2026) Nous, Section 9: provenance-capped belief updating
finding: Trust taken from the source channel (tool output, scraped web) and capped by min(provenance, content) resisted a flood of false observations. Trust inferred from wording was easy to game. Laundering poison through a trusted intermediary defeated simple tiers unless taint was tracked.
numbers: Attack success, 400 trials per cell, 4 trusted observations against M poison observations on a channel of provenance 0.2: provenance-capped 0% at M=1,3,10,50; last-write-wins 100% at all M; content-trusted 0,0,100,100; append-majority 100%. Authoritative-style poison earned reliability 0.96 vs 0.25 hedged. Guarantee holds for channel trust <=0.5 and fails above 0.55. Cost: a true correction through a 0.3 channel dropped accuracy from 100% to 54%. Laundering: attack success back to 100% without taint tracking.
limits: Provenance tiers assigned by an oracle, synthetic simulation plus a minimal coding harness, taint tracking not implemented. The poison model is the author's own.
agent_relevance: Entrenchment from provenance (executed output over model assertion) is defensible as a rule, but a cap also blocks true late corrections from low-tier sources. Propagate provenance through the agent's own summaries.

source: Singh (2026) Nous, Section 5 and related work: LoCoMo ablation and judge fragility
finding: Replacing the Bayesian update by last-write-wins did not lower accuracy on LoCoMo, because ordinary conversational QA has few contradictions. The paper cites an outside audit saying the LoCoMo LLM judge accepts many wrong answers.
numbers: Ablation on 3 conversations, 385 questions. Same outputs scored 59.97 (generous LLM judge) vs 32.45 (strict token-F1), a 27.5-point macro gap. Cited audit (Penfield Labs 2026, secondhand): judge accepts up to 63% of intentionally wrong answers; about 6.4% of LoCoMo ground-truth answers contain errors.
limits: The audit figures are quoted from the paper, not opened. Small subset. Bears on gap 10: published memory scores depend on the judge, so cross-paper comparison is unsafe.
agent_relevance: Treat self-reported memory-benchmark gains as unconfirmed unless scored with a strict metric. Revise tests need real contradictions.

source: He and Yu (2026) Stored Is Not Supported: typed provenance and assertion guardrails
finding: Formal design that separates storing a claim from being allowed to assert it, with a provenance graph, staleness flags and a generate-verify-revise release gate. Evaluated only on a hand-written conformance suite, not on a language model.
numbers: 24 conformance cases. Unsafe-release rate: typed mediation 0 of 19 unsafe opportunities; flat/prior rule 19 of 19; source-tag rule 18 of 19. 5 of 5 supported controls kept.
limits: Validates the authors' own rules; they state it is not an end-to-end LLM evaluation. No replication, no model numbers.
agent_relevance: Gives a checklist for what a candidate-claim record needs (origin, dependency lineage, validity time) but is no evidence that it improves LLM revision.

source: Olausson et al. (2023/2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Gap 5. With the model giving its own feedback on test failures, repair gives small, uneven gains and often loses to sampling more at equal budget. The bottleneck is the quality of the feedback that locates the fault.
numbers: APPS 300 tasks (180 interview, 60 competition, 60 intro); GPT-3.5, GPT-4, CodeLlama-13b. Relative gains over baseline: GPT-4 APPS up to 8%; GPT-3.5 marginal except up to 34% on competition problems; CodeLlama HumanEval up to 10%. Equal budget: 10 initial samples with 1 repair each = 1.05x of pass@20; 2 initial with 10 repairs each = 0.97x of pass@22. Repair success: GPT-4 10.8% (APPS), 49.6% (HumanEval).
quote: Self-repair is not a silver bullet for code generation
limits: Read through an HTML rendering, first 100,000 of 137,096 characters. 2023 models (gpt-3.5-0301, gpt-4-0314). Absolute pass rates only in heatmaps.
agent_relevance: At equal tokens, resampling can match repair. A forced Revise state must be justified by a trustworthy fault signal, not by the model's own critique.

source: Olausson et al. (2023/2024) human-feedback study
finding: Same paper, controlled swap of who writes the feedback. Human feedback on the failing program made GPT-4 repair succeed far more often than GPT-4's own feedback, so the located error, not the rewriting, was the limit.
numbers: 16 participants, 40 failing GPT-4 programs, 25 repair candidates per feedback string. Repair success 33.3% (GPT-4 feedback) vs 52.6% (human), 1.58x. By difficulty: intro 42.64 vs 62.21; interview 19.33 vs 45.67; competition 3.67 vs 14.67. Inaccurate feedback: GPT-4 32 of 80, human 7 of 80.
limits: Small participant pool (15 graduate students, 1 engineer), one repair model, 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Supports feeding S5 concrete located evidence (failing test, trace line) and not a free-form self-critique.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Gap 5. Execution feedback from unit tests is the largest driver of repair gains. An explanation of the failure adds a little. With no code execution, gains are small or negative.
numbers: TransCoder (560 problems): Codex 80.4 baseline to 91.6 with unit-test feedback and 92.5 with test plus explanation; GPT-4 77.3 to 88.8 and 90.4. MBPP (500 problems): GPT-4 72.8 to 80.6 (test) and 80.4 (test plus explanation); Codex simple feedback 61.4 to 68.2. Spider with no tests: Codex 81.3 to 84.1 only with explanation, simple feedback +0.0; GPT-4 73.2 to 73.6. No execution, MBPP Codex simple feedback 57.6, below the 61.4 baseline.
limits: Read through an HTML rendering, first 100,000 of 128,994 characters. The paper's own tables disagree slightly (Codex MBPP 75.6 vs 73.6). Older models. Trace feedback mixed (Codex TransCoder 87.9 vs 92.5 for test plus explanation).
agent_relevance: Real execution output as the contradicting evidence is what pays. An explanation step adds roughly 1 to 3 points when no tests exist. Matches the schema's evidence-gated Revise.

source: Li (2026) Decomposing LLM Self-Correction: accuracy-correction paradox
finding: On GSM8K errors, detecting its own error did not predict fixing it. Model-generated location hints lowered correction for two of three models.
numbers: 500 problems per model, 346 errors total (DeepSeek 30, GPT-3.5 168, Claude-3-Haiku 148). Detection 56.7 / 81.5 / 10.1%. Intrinsic correction 16.7 / 26.8 / 29.1%. With model-made hint 26.7 / 15.5 / 12.8%. Iterative up to 3 rounds 20.0 / 67.9 / 60.8%.
limits: Only 30 errors for DeepSeek. Old small models. Hints are model-made, not ground truth. Error-depth claim is inferred, not measured. Claude baseline accuracy given as 73.3% and 70.4% in two places. The 'iterative' figure is compared with a detection rate, not like for like.
agent_relevance: Self-located faults are unreliable, in line with Tyen. Do not let the agent pick the faulty belief from introspection alone.

source: Deng et al. (2026) DeFA: Dependency-Guided Failure Attribution for LLM Agents
finding: Gap 5, location accuracy in long agent traces. A dependency graph over trace steps raises exact-step attribution over seven baselines, yet exact localisation stays hard.
numbers: Who&When 184 trajectories: exact step 52.7 (GLM-5.2), 48.9 (DeepSeek-V4-Pro), 50.0 (Qwen3.8-Max); within 3 steps about 70; gains 7.6 to 9.8 points over best baseline. Who&When Pro 300 trajectories: exact step 76.3 to 80.3, within 3 steps 92.7 to 95.3. Trajectories of 33 to 130 steps: 17.2% exact.
limits: Authors' own method on an extended benchmark. Dependency recovery depends on the model reading the trace.
agent_relevance: Step-level blame in a long run is right about half the time and about 17% on long traces. A revise gate should drop dependents of a flagged claim and keep a cheap rollback, not trust one-shot blame.

source: Mukherjee et al. (2025) Premise-Augmented Reasoning Chains Improve Error Identification
finding: Gap 5. Giving the checker each step's premises (a dependency link) raises step error identification.
numbers: 607 chains (203 correct, 214 natural negatives, 190 synthetic). Average over four sources: Llama 3.1 70B 68.54 to 76.60; Qwen 2.5 72B 63.83 to 77.70; GPT-4o 68.25 to 77.16; Llama 3.1 8B 58.33 to 61.34. Accumulation errors, Llama 70B 12.0 to 57.54. ProcessBench: Qwen 7B GSM8K F1 47.2 to 47.0; Llama 70B 66.1 to 78.6.
limits: Labels from o1-Preview, 10% hand-checked (4 premise and 5 error disagreements in 71). Bias toward calling steps correct. Accuracy on correct steps falls. Cost O(n^2).
agent_relevance: Dependency tracking makes the faulty-step search better, which supports recording which claim rests on which.

source: Jiang et al. (2026) Exact Feedback Is Not Control: text-based closed-loop revision
finding: Gap 7 (empirical). With perfect, complete verifier feedback, models still often repeat the same output or fall into short cycles. Many failed revision loops are stuck, not slowly improving.
numbers: 19 model configurations, 3 constraint families x 480 cases, 27,360 trajectories, budget 8 revisions. Final joint success 17.4% (Qwen3 1.7B) to 99.8% (GPT-5.6 Sol); local mean 39.3%, API mean 83.3%. Among failed runs output recurrence 84.8 / 78.7 / 90.2%; fixed points or cycles 69.0 / 57.6 / 79.5%. Adjusted odds ratio for later recovery after prior recurrence 0.047.
limits: Text-length and lexical constraints only, not belief revision. Deterministic verifier. It does not compare lexicographic with restrained operators.
agent_relevance: If the same claim keeps being re-proposed after the same failed check, treat it as a fixed point and change something. Gives a measurable oscillation signal.

source: Jiang et al. (2026) history-reset intervention
finding: Clearing the failed-attempt history at a matched recurrent state helps the next step a lot but final success only a little.
numbers: Next-step escape +42.2 points (Llama 3.1 8B) and +49.2 (GLM-4 9B). Final success +10.8 points (to 21.7%) and +5.0 (to 8.3%). Matched recurrent states; primary analysis covers two models on exact-length tasks.
limits: Two models, one task family; other cells descriptive. Read the first 100,000 of 171,132 characters.
agent_relevance: Partly agrees with Chowdhury's reset-beats-history (0.52 vs 0.11) in a different setting but shows the end gain is small. Reset is a rescue move, not a cure. Break-even at equal tokens (gap 9) is not measured.

source: Xu and Wu (2026) Stale Instruction Files Override the Code in Coding Agents: A One-Sentence Fix
finding: Gaps 1 and 6. Two 2026 coding agents with tools followed a stale instruction file over the actual code. One added sentence telling them to follow the code when the two disagree reversed it.
numbers: 40 Python projects, 16 convention types, 320 runs (2 agents x 2 conditions x 2 repeats). Without the sentence 90.1% (649/720) of choices matched the stale file and 4.2% the code. Claude Code named the conflict in 79 of 80 runs and still followed the file in 86.2%. Codex CLI rewrote existing code in 20 of 80 runs; project tests failed in 17. With the sentence 91.4% (658/720) matched the code; tests passed in all 160 runs vs 89.4%.
limits: Preprint, small synthetic projects, one unattended run per task, two agents, conflict judged by a second model. The sentence is a prompt rule, not a staged Revise state, and there is no equal-token comparison.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a one-line provenance rule (executable code beats prose) flips agent behaviour. Models already notice the conflict; they lack a rule for which side wins.

source: Ma et al. (2026) Sycophancy Suppression Can Impair Rational Updating
finding: Gap 6. Training or steering a model to resist pressure also cuts its updating on valid evidence; the two behaviours share internal parts. No one-gate fix by training was found.
numbers: 4 open models, 4 datasets (TruthfulQA, PopQA, EX-FEVER, AQuA). Before intervention, unsupported yielding 70.5 / 73.6 / 49.9 / 17.1% (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-3-4B, Qwen3-8B); rational updating on evidence 60.7 / 64.1 / 59.8 / 53.7%. Anti-pressure DPO on EX-FEVER with Llama-3.1: yielding down 32.9 points, rational updating down 48.9 to 53.7. Orthogonal steering raised selective settings from 5 to 10 of 36. Shared neurons 32 to 45 of 50.
limits: Open 3B to 8B models only. Evidence always correct and golden. Steering only on TruthfulQA. Split sizes not in the part read (first 100,000 of 129,803 characters).
agent_relevance: Do not fix over-flipping by making the agent stubborn in general. Put the discrimination in the scaffold (is there new executed evidence?) and not in the weights.

source: Shapira, Cheng and Orgad (2026) Is Sycophancy a Form of In-Context Updating?
finding: Gap 6 with frontier 2026 models. Adoption of a stated claim depends strongly on its source and stated reliability. Reducing sycophancy by pruning also reduces updating from reliable sources.
numbers: Frontier set: GPT-5.6 Terra, GPT-5.6 Luna, Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5. Opus 5 vs Sonnet 5 user-claim adoption 21% vs 78%, source adoption 27% vs 98%. Correlation between sycophancy reduction and source-updating reduction r=0.87 (frontier), 0.90 (open weight). Reliability levels 20/50/90%. 1,000 weights pruned per open model.
limits: N per condition not in the part read (first 100,000 of 155,551 characters). MMLU-Pro factual multiple choice only. Pruning only on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B; frontier results are behavioural. Evidence and pressure are not cleanly separated.
agent_relevance: Source label and stated reliability change what models accept, so a candidate list that carries provenance and reliability is a lever the model already responds to.

source: Elio and Pelletier (1997) Belief change as propositional update, Cognitive Science 21
finding: Gap 4, human side, independent lab, 12 years before Walsh and Johnson-Laird. People abandoned the conditional more than the ground fact, more so with story content than symbols, and did not follow any of four formal minimal-change definitions.
numbers: Five experiments (sample sizes not in the abstract). Conditionals more readily abandoned than ground sentences in Experiments 1 to 3. Experiments 4 and 5: none of four model-theoretic minimal-change definitions matched. Preferred revision kept only sentences with a stable, unambiguous truth value.
limits: Only the abstract text (via Crossref) was read; the publisher page returned 403. It does not test explanation-first. The pattern differs for modus ponens and modus tollens.
agent_relevance: Supports not hard-coding minimal change as the human-like rule. Says nothing about what is best for an LLM.

source: Vasileiou, Rago, Martinez and Yeoh (2025) How Do People Revise Inconsistent Beliefs?
finding: Gap 4, human side, another independent lab. Participants mostly changed or dropped general rules, not specific facts, and revised far more than the minimum, even after being shown a disabling-condition explanation.
numbers: Prolific, Exp 1 N=62, Exp 2 N=60, Exp 3 N=60; 9 scenarios. Non-minimal revisions 83.37% (Exp 1), 85.51% (Exp 2; 91.36% for two-rule problems), 67.16% (Exp 3). Mean changes per problem 2.14 / 2.87 / 3.81 where two were needed.
limits: No formal predictive model, entrenchment not tested, informal minimality definition, 11 to 13% of responses unclassifiable, no stated effect sizes. It does not test whether the explanation causes the choice. No LLM part.
agent_relevance: A second independent source for non-minimal, rule-first human revision. Whether explanation-first helps LLMs is still untested.

source: Suzgun et al. (2024) Belief in the Machine: KaBLE
finding: Models handle another person's false belief much better than a first-person false belief, a gap in belief-status handling.
numbers: 13,000 questions, 13 tasks, 15 models, zero-shot. First-person confirmation of false beliefs 54.4% vs 92.1% for true ones; third-person false 80.7%. Second-guessing a first-person belief: 88.6% true vs 44.7% false. GPT-4 22.0% on false first-person confirmation.
limits: 2024 models, single prompt template, exact-match scoring, atomic epistemic tasks. Not a revision test.
agent_relevance: Context only: a model has trouble holding a statement as believed but false. Mark claims in the base with a status, not just text.

source: Jenkins (2026) AGM-Bench, ICLR 2026 workshop page, second attempt
finding: Gap 3 stays open. The page again gives only the abstract with no per-postulate table. The OpenReview full text is blocked by a verification challenge (HTTP 403) and arXiv search found no copy.
numbers: 2,400 synthetic scenarios, 7 frontier models, 6 AGM postulates plus Darwiche-Pearl. Qualitative only: Success and Consistency high; Inclusion and Preservation often broken; reasoning-trained models (o3-mini, DeepSeek-R1) better in one step, degrade faster over iterations.
limits: Single author, workshop paper. No numbers retrievable here. o3-mini and R1 are not 2026 frontier.
agent_relevance: Treat 'models break minimal change' as plausible but unmeasured. Run our own Inclusion and Preservation check.

source: Lee et al. (2026) InterventionBench, Findings of EMNLP
finding: Gap 8, an outside benchmark by other authors for changing a goal mid-task. Every intervention type lowered agent performance; additions were hardest.
numbers: 2,250 intervention instances on AppWorld and WebArena, 12 LLM agents, 9 intervention types (3 operations x 3 goal components).
limits: Only the abstract page was read; no scores, no model list, no test of dependency propagation. A benchmark, not a test of Chowdhury's method.
agent_relevance: A usable outside testbed for any Revise-on-new-information claim. The dependency-propagation gain still has no independent replication.

source: Wang and Wang (2026) The Observability Gap: output-level human feedback for coding agents
finding: Gaps 5 and 7. With feedback only on the rendered output, a coding agent loop stayed stuck. Adding one diagnostic code-level constraint fixed it.
numbers: Blender scene task. Groups A to C (coarse, quantitative, algorithm named): 0 of 10 runs each succeeded; collision avoidance failed every time. Group D (code-level constraint): converged in 3 of 3 tests within 3 cycles.
limits: 10 runs per group, one task, one evaluator, one model family, no statistics, Group D a diagnostic probe.
agent_relevance: Locating the fault at code level, not describing symptoms, broke the loop. Weak (tiny N) but points the same way as d05 and d06.

source: Qian et al. (2026) Toward User-Conditioned Evaluation of Personal LLM Agents under Temporal Interventions
finding: Gap 8. A position paper: none of 15 public agent protocols tests changed or stale user state under all four conditions. Their simulations used scripted policies, not LLMs.
numbers: 15 protocols coded, mean agreement .947 (Gwet AC1 .898); none met all four conditions. Simulated: static policy failed at the horizon in 100%, reactive 15 to 17%, versioned 1%. 200 rollouts per cell. LLM check: 20 trials per condition, compatibility only.
limits: No real agent results; numbers come from scripted failure probabilities.
agent_relevance: Confirms the benchmark gap and does not answer it. No independent test of propagate-on-update exists on a free-running agent.
